exact_spans: The inverse design of metasurfaces aims to directly determine the optimal structures that achieve desired electromagnetic (EM) responses. Existing inverse design methods face two key limitations: incomplete design specifications and non-uniqueness effects, which hinder accurate and automated inverse design. A unified machine-learning framework is proposed to generate optimized metasurface structures based on real-world design specifications for addressing these two limitations. Unlike conventional approaches that require full plots of EM response curves over the desired frequency band, our method is compatible with unformatted design specifications, such as single values that summarize the characteristics within the frequency band of interest. These design specifications are formatted into feature vectors. The feature vectors are combined with arbitrary Gaussian noise vectors and fed into a conditional decoder to reconstruct full plots of the desired EM responses. To mitigate the effects of non-uniqueness, how non-uniqueness causes non-differentiability of the loss functions and deteriorates the convergence of inverse modeling is analyzed. Based on this analysis, a Gaussian distribution latent space and a pre-trained forward model-based loss function are integrated to mitigate the non-uniqueness effects and ensure robust generation of optimized metasurface structures via an encoder. This framework is validated by designing a linear-to-circular polarization converter metasurface, and its robustness is further investigated by doubling and tripling the original design parameter range. Comparative results demonstrate that our approach enables efficient and automated inverse design of metasurfaces, reducing the average time needed per design process by 95% and 7% compared with genetic-algorithm-based and forward-model-based methods, respectively. Its performance is maintained by increasing the training data proportionally when the design parameter range expands. This framework can be extended to multi-objective optimization and diverse electromagnetic structures, bridging real-world constraints with high-performance metasurface designs.
evidence_packets.source_title: Unified Machine-Learning Framework for Automated Inverse Design of Metasurfaces

exact_spans: Advances in design and nanofabrication are enabling the ability to realize nanophotonic structures that achieve optical functionalities not possible with conventional devices. Some of the most interesting structures being developed are based on metasurfaces comprised of sub-wavelength unit cells intelligently patterned to locally manipulate an electromagnetic wavefront in a desired way. However, designing a metasurface to achieve a specific set of desired functionalities is extremely challenging especially in the presence of coupling between unit cells, which can affect system performance and lead to unexpected optical aberrations. To overcome this challenge, designers typically employ only canonical structures (e.g., loaded-dipoles, v-antennas, split-ring resonators) to synthesize a metasurface to achieve their desired functionality. However, metadevices based on these canonical structures do not always achieve optimal performance especially when broadband and/or wide-field-of-view functionality is desired. Additionally, different material combinations as well as fabrication effects and tolerances can make the optimal unit cell topology selection difficult. Therefore, the ability to generate a diverse set of unintuitive metasurface unit cells and evaluate their electromagnetic behaviors for achieving a specific functionality is highly desirable. Moreover, doing so in an efficient and intelligent manner is extremely important in order to maintain a tractable inverse design process. To this end, we employ a custom nanoantenna unit cell topology generation routine in conjunction with robust state-of-the-art multi-objective and surrogate-assisted optimization algorithms to find optimal designs that achieve an arbitrary number of user-specified performance criteria. Finally, when paired with advanced full-wave forward solvers these design and optimization algorithms enable an efficient inverse design toolkit for high performance metasurface synthesis.
evidence_packets.source_title: Metasurface synthesis through multi-objective optimization aided inverse-design

exact_spans: With modern nanofabrication technology, researchers and companies can reliably produce 3-dimensional patterns with feature sizes much smaller than the wavelength of visible light. The ability to do this in a scalable fashion brings nanophotonic research into the realm of commercial technology. For example, metasurfaces achieve high optical performance in fractions of the thickness of traditional bulky optical components and can be designed for unique, custom functionalities. By expanding the design space beyond the metasurface regime and allowing for photonic designs in full three dimensions, we can further increase the degrees of freedom at our disposal. This new design space is complex and inherently involves multiply scattering structures. In order to efficiently search for good solutions, we use an inverse design procedure based on the adjoint variable method. Taking advantage of this large design space, we can computationally optimize multi-functional meta-optical devices that achieve novel functionalities in minimal footprints. We demonstrate wavelength splitting photonic filters with application to color filter arrays on modern-day image sensors. These filters are designed to replace absorbing filters and instead re-route colors to specific sensor locations, thus recovering previously lost transmission. We show that these devices work with a variety of realistic fabrication restrictions and demonstrate their abilities experimentally in the microwave regime where we can realize layered devices via simple techniques like 3D printing. Finally, we comment on potential future applications and avenues where inverse design can help solve inherently difficult engineering challenges in nanophotonics.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse design approaches for volumetric meta-optics

exact_spans: The modern design of advanced functional materials or surfaces has increasingly undergone miniaturization and integration, so as to implement multiple functions using the same aperture. Metasurfaces, as an emerging kind of artificial functional surface, have provided unprecedented freedom in manipulating electomagnetic (EM) waves upon two-dimensional surfaces. It is desirable that the aperture of metasurfaces can be multiplexed with a number of functions for EM waves. Based on previous research, an artificial neural network-forward design can achieve an inverse design. In this paper, we propose an inverse design method of multiplexing metasurface apertures. A deep learning network (DLN) is trained to serve as a forward model for a genetic algorithm (GA), that is, a deep-leaning-forward genetic algorithm (DLF-GA). With the DLF-GA model, the phase of meta-atoms can be predicted for orthogonally linearly polarized waves simultaneously. The DLN was trained by a data set consisting of 70 000 samples with an accuracy of 95% on the test data. To demonstrate the competency of this method, we demonstrate the design of a multiplexed metasurface that can achieve focusing and diffuse scattering for polarization. The metasurface, which consists of 24 × 24 meta-atoms, can be generated monolithically with the input phase profile. A prototype was fabricated and measured. The predicted, simulated, and measured results are well consistent and underscore the validity of this inverse design method. This method provides an efficient and accurate method for the fast design of multiplexed metasurfaces and will find applications in microwave engineering such as in satellite communications.
evidence_packets.source_title: Multiplexing the aperture of a metasurface: inverse design via deep-learning-forward genetic algorithm

exact_spans: Metasurfaces composed of spatially arranged ultrathin subwavelength elements are promising photonic devices for manipulating optical wavefronts, with potential applications in holography, metalens, and multiplexing com-munications. Finding microstructures that meet light modulation requirements is always a challenge in designing metasurfaces, where parameter sweep, gradient-based inverse design, and topology optimization are the most commonly used design methods in which the massive electromagnetic iterations require the design computational cost and are sometimes prohibitive. Herein, we propose a fast inverse design method that combines a physics-based neural network surrogate model (NNSM) with an optimization algorithm. The NNSM, which can generate an accurate electromagnetic response from the geometric topologies of the meta-atoms, is constructed for electromagnetic iterations, and the optimization algorithm is used to search for the on-demand meta-atoms from the phase library established by the NNSM to realize an inverse design. This method addresses two important prob-lems in metasurface design: fast and accurate electromagnetic wave phase prediction and inverse design through a single phase-shift value. As a proof-of-concept, we designed an orbital angular momentum (de)multiplexer based on a phase-type metasurface, and 200 Gbit/s quadrature-phase shift-keying signals were successfully transmitted with a bit error rate approaching 1 . 67 × 10 − 6 . Because the design is mainly based on an optimization algorithm, it can address the " one-to-many " inverse problem in other micro/nano devices such as integrated photonic circuits, waveguides, and nano-antennas.
evidence_packets.source_title: Neural network-based surrogate model for inverse design of metasurfaces

exact_spans: A design method for second-order differentiators based on metasurface, integrating spatial-frequency domain modulation with data-driven inverse optimization, achieves optical second-order differentiation functionality through rigorous modeling using the angular spectrum approach. First, a training dataset is constructed based on Gaussian beam propagation theory, forming a data-driven design framework constrained by the target Laplacian differential optical field. Subsequently, a differential evolution algorithm is embedded within the angular spectrum method's physical propagation model to perform a global search for the phase mask. At each iteration, errors are evaluated by simulating real free-space propagation to obtain the optimal phase mask satisfying second-order differential characteristics. Subsequently, FDTD simulations scanned the radius of the micro-nano unit structure at a fixed height to construct a radius-phase database. A particle swarm optimization algorithm then searched this database to identify structural parameters corresponding to the optimal phase mask, yielding a complete optimal radius-phase matrix and achieving precise inversion of the metasurface unit structure. Finally, the metasurface is constructed in FDTD for electromagnetic simulation verification. Results demonstrate that the structure generates clear and stable second-order differential responses at a single wavelength, proving the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed data-driven inverse design method for optical operator device design.
evidence_packets.source_title: Data-driven inverse design of metasurface-based optical second-order differentiators

exact_spans: The diverse range of shapes enabled by modern nanofabrication techniques makes it challenging to identify the most optimal design for a desired optical response. While deep learning-based approaches are being increasingly explored for inverse design (especially for optical metasurfaces), they have mostly been limited to small design subsets that constrain the shapes, thicknesses, or parameters like pitch, incident angle, etc. Scalability of such techniques to the full design space accessible to modern nanofabrication remains a challenge due to the difficulty of training models which retain acceptable generalization across wider design spaces. We explore the possibility of using active learning techniques for sample-efficient model training and surrogate-driven inverse design. Specifically, we consider the inverse design of periodic optical metasurfaces with 36 diverse shape classes and broad variations in thickness and pitch. Our results demonstrate that an active learning-driven approach to inverse design can give comparable performance to random-dataset trained models with a substantial (up to 82%) reduction in training dataset generation. The inverse design capability is seen across diverse spectral filter optimization tasks with the added benefit of providing multiple solutions in a single run. As a model- and training-paradigm-agnostic dataset reduction technique, our approach enables deep learning-based inverse design to scale to increasingly larger design spaces.
evidence_packets.source_title: Active learning for efficient nanophotonics inverse design in large and diverse design spaces.

exact_spans: The functional and optimal design of optical metasurfaces poses great challenges, particularly in situations requiring multifunctionalities. The conventional forward design relies on a priori knowledge, which limits the development of metasurfaces with customized functions. Inverse design has achieved major breakthroughs in developing new optical functionalities but has been hindered by inevitably invoking a full-wave electromagnetic solver, subjected to low efficiency, slow convergence, and being hard to implement. Here, we propose a general and computationally efficient inverse-design framework based on multipole decomposition and adjoint optimization. By this method, we demonstrate an achromatic metalens working across the visible and near-infrared band with a bandwidth over 400 nm. We also show the design of the metasurface for multiplexed focusing at the RGB wavelength, and the metasurface for stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy, which generates a tightly focusing point at the excitation beam wavelength and doughnut-shaped focus for the STED beam wavelength. Our scheme could be further improved to include more geometrical degrees of freedom and show great applications in free-space diffractive optics and deep diffractive neural network.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Design of Multifunctional Metasurface Based on Multipole Decomposition and the Adjoint Method

exact_spans: Electromagnetic metasurfaces pave the way for manipulating electromagnetic waves across the entire electromagnetic spectrum and applications. Nevertheless, the process of finding an optimal design for a desired response poses great challenges. Conventionally, this design approach depends on elaborate investigation of the electromagnetic properties of the metasurface in hand, supported by extensive full wave simulations that are extremely computationally demanding. This work presents a comparative analysis of three global optimization algorithms, namely Genetic Algorithm (GA), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and Flower Pollination Algorithm (FPA) for the inverse design of metasurfaces based on a forward machine learning model, XGBoost, as a surrogate for computationally expensive simulations. The proposed algorithms are applied to several objective error functions including Mean Squared Error (MSE), Integral Squared Error (ISE), and Integral of Absolute Error (IAE). Additionally, the work highlights the implementation of linear to circular polarization conversion for a single frequency. This work offers valuable insights for selecting appropriate algorithms and objective error functions for the inverse design of metasurfaces.
evidence_packets.source_title: Metasurface Inverse Design: Global Optimization and Machine Learning Integration

exact_spans: The electromagnetic properties of meta-atoms determine the degree of freedom of the transmitted electromagnetic waves manipulated by metasurfaces. However, there are singular point mutations in the mapping between the electromagnetic properties and geometric structure of meta-atoms, which increases the difficulty of design. In the paper, we present a meta-atoms inverse design approach based on deep residual networks combined with electromagnetic properties classification. We designed the network to predict the geometry of meta-atoms from the amplitude and phase of the transmission coefficients. By combining electromagnetic property classification, the network effectively solves the problem of inaccurate predictions caused by singular point mutations and reduces training data. The mean square error of all parameters in the data set is less than 0.23. Furthermore, we also designed the holographic imaging metasurfaces to verify network reliability. The network proved to be a new tool for the inverse design of meta-atoms.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Design of Metasurface Holography on Deep Residual Networks

exact_spans: A hybrid framework for solving the non-uniqueness problem in the inverse design of isomorphic metasurfaces is proposed. The framework consists of a representation learning (RL) module and a variational autoencoder-particle swarm optimization (VAE-PSO) algorithm module. The RL module is used to reduce the complex high-dimensional space into a low-dimensional space with obvious features, with the purpose of eliminating the many-to-one relationship between the original design space and response space. The VAE-PSO algorithm first encodes all meta-atoms into a continuous latent space through VAE and then applies PSO to search for an optimized latent vector whose corresponding metasurface fulfills the target response. This framework gives the solution paradigm of the ideal non-uniqueness situation, simplifies the complexity of the network, improves the running speed of the PSO algorithm, and obtains the global optimal solution with 94% accuracy on the test set.
evidence_packets.source_title: An Inverse Design Framework for Isotropic Metasurfaces Based on Representation Learning

exact_spans: Conventional metasurface design methods usually require a lot of computational resources and time, meaning they fail to satisfy the efficient, rapid design on demand. On account of this, we branch out of the conventional metasurface design methods by attempting to relate the emerging discipline of artificial intelligence to a traditional physical area. With our method, named AMID, metasurface structures are designed inversely where they can be computed directly by simply proposing and inputting the desired design targets into AMID. AMID greatly simplifies conventional methods that call for not only sufficient professional knowledge but also trial and error through simulation softwares. According to the design results, unit cells of metasurfaces are successfully computed, which verifies the availability of AMID and improves the design efficiency in the meanwhile.
evidence_packets.source_title: Metasurface inverse design using machine learning approaches

exact_spans: Metamaterial and metasurface devices (i.e., meta-devices) have shown tremendous potential for disrupting conventional RF and optical system design due to their ability to tailor the propagation of electromagnetic radiation in a desired fashion. Meta-devices are generally synthesized from "meta-atom" building blocks which are optimized to meet a certain set of user-designed performance criteria. Meta-atom optimization often requires the use of full-wave electromagnetic solvers which can make the process computationally challenging, especially when a large number of design parameters are used to define the meta-atoms. To this end, inverse-design strategies based on multi-objective optimization and deep learning which seek to efficiently explore the vast space afforded by nanofabricated meta-devices are presented.
evidence_packets.source_title: Optimization and Deep Learning Techniques for Nanophotonic Inverse-Design

exact_spans: The scattering enhancement technique has shown prominent potential in various regimes such as satellite communication, Radar Cross Section (RCS) camouflage, and remote sensing. Currently, the scattering enhancement devices based on the metasurface have shown advantages in light weight and better performance. These metasurfaces always possess complex structure, it is hard to achieve through the tradition trial-and-error method which relies on the full-wave numerical simulation. In this paper, a new method combining the machine learning and the evolution optimization algorithm is proposed to design the metasurface retroreflector (MRF) for arbitrary direction incident wave. In this method, a predicting model and a generative inverse design model are constructed and trained, the predicting model is used to evaluate the fitness of each offspring in the genetic algorithm (GA), the generative model is used to initialize the first offspring of the GA by inverse generate the MRF based on the requirements of the designer. With the assistance of these two machine learning models, the evolution optimization algorithm is employed to find the optimal design of the MRF. This approach enables automatic solution of electromagnetic inverse design problems and opens the way to facilitate the optimization of other metadevices.
evidence_packets.source_title: Machine-learning-assisted inverse design of scattering enhanced metasurface.

exact_spans: Metasurface provides an unprecedented means to manipulate electromagnetic waves within a two-dimensional planar structure. Traditionally, the design of meta-atom follows the pattern-to-phase paradigm, which requires a time-consuming brute-forcing process. In this work, we present a fast inverse meta-atom design method for the phase-to-pattern mapping by combining the deep neural network (DNN) and genetic algorithm (GA). The trained classification DNN with an accuracy of 92% controls the population generated by the GA within an arbitrary preset small phase range, which could greatly enhance the optimization efficiency with less iterations and a higher accuracy. As proof-of-concept demonstrations, two reflective functional metasurfaces including an orbital angular momentum generator and a metalens have been numerically investigated. The simulated results agree very well with the design goals. In addition, the metalens is also experimentally validated. The proposed method could pave a new avenue for the fast design of the meta-atoms and functional meta-devices.
evidence_packets.source_title: Phase-to-pattern inverse design for a fast realization of a functional metasurface by combining a deep neural network and a genetic algorithm.

exact_spans: An electromagnetic inverse source algorithm, which was developed to infer the macroscopic properties of metasurfaces from desired power patterns for 2-D wave propagation, is extended to the 3-D configuration. This is pursued in conjunction with some simplifying assumptions that reduce the associated 3-D full-vectorial inverse metasurface design problem to a 3-D scalar one. This inversion algorithm takes the desired power patterns on two perpendicular far-field cuts, and outputs the required equivalent currents on the surface of the metasurface. The required metasurface macroscopic properties can be subsequently found. Finally, a discussion on the presence of surface waves in this formulation is presented which facilitates meeting the local power conservation constraint.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Metasurface Design From 3-D Desired Power Patterns on Two Cuts

exact_spans: Deep learning not only brings great changes to the field of image processing and voice recognition, but it also gradually affects the design of electromagnetic devices. Here, we propose an inverse design method based on neural networks to automatically output metasurface structure with controllable working bandwidth for linear polarization-conversion. As a result, relative bandwidth can be flexibly selected from 0 to 76% in the range of 7–20 GHz. The proposed method provides a platform to accelerate the on-demand design of meta-polarizer and other versatile devices for real-world applications.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Design of Metasurface Polarization Convertor with Controllable Bandwidth

exact_spans: According to the mechanism of searching for feasible solutions, the iterative EM metamaterial inverse design methods have been primarily categorized into two main branches: gradient-based methods and gradient-free methods. The concept of gradients is fundamental in optimization theory as it indicates the direction and rate at which a function increases most rapidly [46]. Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of directly applying gradient descent approach to metamaterial inverse design [47,48]. Additionally, TO [36][37][38], which has garnered considerable attention, is based on gradient approach. TO divides the design space into discretized elements, treating material distribution in each element as design variable, thereby offering substantial design flexibility [38,49]. Its computational consumption does not significantly increase with the system dimensionality, making it adept at handling large design degrees of freedom [50]. However, as a gradient-based optimization method, TO requires welldefined, continuous, and differentiable system models, rendering it unsuitable for solving optimization problems where the gradient information is unavailable. Although density-based TO has incorporated effective techniques such as filtering and projection to ensure manufacturability and mesh-convergence [51][52][53][54], integrating geometry and fabrication constraints into the optimization process remains intricate. Furthermore, engineering inverse problems are often non-convex, meaning that there is no guarantee that the locally optimized solution found by TO is also globally optimized [35]. In contrast, gradient-free optimization methods, such as genetic algorithms (GAs) [55], particle swarm optimization (PSO) [56], and covariance matrix adaptive evolutionary strategy (CMA-ES) [57], etc can overcome some of the implementing limitations of gradient-based methods. These EAs, based on principles of biological evolution or swarm intelligence, use heuristic update laws to discover global optimization solutions, and are compatible with discretized objective functions [58]. One notable advantage of EAs lies in the easy-to-apply implementation, particularly beneficial for engineers unfamiliar with the derivation of numerical simulation equations. Typically, it is only required to calculate the objective function value through graphical user interfacebased modeling simulation software to carry out the optimization process.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse design of electromagnetic metamaterials: from iterative to deep learning-based methods

exact_spans: Discriminative models bypass the repeated EM inputoutput simulations, often the bottlenecks of the optimization schemes reviewed in the previous section. Discriminative models are essentially unique configurations of deep learning architectures that learn the relationship between designs in the parameter space and their optical responses (reflection, transmission, amplitude or phase) [85][86][87][88][89][90][91]. Based on the study of plasmonic nanostructures, Malkiel et al. [92] introduced a bidirectional network composed of geometry-predicting-network (GPN) and spectra-predicting-network (SPN). The authors train the GPN in a supervised manner with a dataset composed of 15,000 randomly generated device layouts containing eight geometrical parameters, including width, height, rotation angle, and the presence of positional elements in the H-shaped framework. Additional to the device data, finite elements simulations (FEM) calculate the corresponding transmission spectra. The GPN predicts the geometrical design parameters by processing 86 sample points from both TE and TM spectra and dispersive material coefficients. After training, the SPN, constructed in a cascade with the GPN output layer, retrieves the spectra from the eight geometrical parameters launched at the input. The network efficiently leverages the limited dataset by using unseen shapes generated by GPN as the training set of SPN. The loss function and gradient propagate to each layer in both networks. The end-to-end training of the network converges within 2 h, after which the time required to complete queries for potential nanostructures lies in the millisecond range. As exemplified in this work, the GPN retrieves classic nanophotonic structures such as nanobars, L-shaped, and split-ring resonators. To efficiently extract the hidden features from nanostructures, the training of a forward model (device-to-response) and an inverse model (response-to-device) is beneficial. Similar to the GPN and SPN introduced above, the two models can be either constructed and trained independently [93] or with inner connections, such as the generative models that will be introduced in the next section.
evidence_packets.source_title: Advancing statistical learning and artificial intelligence in nanophotonics inverse design

exact_spans: We present a machine learning-based photonics design strategy centered on encoding image colors with material and structural data. Given input target spectra, our model can accurately determine the optimal metasurface class, materials, and structure.
evidence_packets.source_title: Conditional Machine Learning-Based Inverse Design Across Multiple Classes of Nanophotonic Structures

exact_spans: In this paper, an inverse-design network that combined neural network is proposed. Compared with traditional inverse network, the proposed network can achieve higher accuracy and efficiency. A reflective metasurface is used as an example to confirm the validity of this method.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Design of Metasurface Using Combined Neural Network and Transfer Function

exact_spans: We show that the free-form inverse design of nanophotonic matasurfaces can be solved with a modified CGAN machine learning method that balances the accuracy of desired optical properties with experimental feasibility.
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Design of Free-Form Metasurfaces with Deep Neural Networks

exact_spans: As a result, heuristic methods often produce target phase profiles or transfer matrices that are not physically realizable. When these idealized designs are projected onto feasible metasurface structures, the mismatch leads to significant deviations in optical behavior and degraded DONN performance. This disconnect between abstract models and physical reality has been a persistent challenge. Efforts to mitigate this issue, e.g., by applying smoothness regularization 9,11 to phase profiles to ease hardware design, have generally been inadequate. While smoother profiles are simpler to implement, they significantly limit DONN expressivity and do not ensure true physical feasibility, often leading to impractical designs. In contrast, simulation-in-the-loop training 28 embeds metasurface optimization directly within the training loop by leveraging adjoint methods. These methods compute analytical gradients via forward and adjoint full-wave electromagnetic simulations. By parameterizing the DONN trainable weights as physical metasurface design variables, such as meta-atom widths, this approach effectively enforces physical feasibility at every training iteration. However, the demanding requirement of solving Maxwell's equations for each metasurface at each iteration makes this approach prohibitively expensive and fundamentally unscalable to the large, high-capacity optical systems needed for advanced AI tasks. To address the feasibility and scalability bottlenecks in DONN training, we propose SP 2 RINT, a physics-aware optimization scheme that progressively enforces Maxwell PDE constraints during training. Unlike prior heuristic or simulation-in-the-loop approaches, SP 2 RINT alternates between relaxed DONN training and inverse metasurface projection, ensuring that learned responses remain physically realizable while maintaining efficient design space exploration. To further reduce the significant computational cost, we develop a patch-wise metasurface simulation strategy. This strategy effectively exploits the locality of meta-atom interactions and inherent spatial frequency limits due to diffraction. This enables scalable metasurface inverse design with nearlinear complexity, facilitating the design of physically implementable and scalable, large-capacity DONNs. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: • We analyze the core limitations of existing DONN training methods, which suffer from modeling inaccuracies and the prohibitive simulation cost.
evidence_packets.source_title: SP2RINT: Spatially-Decoupled Physics-Inspired Progressive Inverse Optimization for Scalable, PDE-Constrained Meta-Optical Neural Network Training

exact_spans: With the increase in design complexity of the metasurface, crosstalk between different channels and work efficiency need to be solved. Therefore, the metasurface still needs continuous improvement and breakthroughs in terms of performance improvement. Currently, the methods to solve the problems of narrow operating frequency and angle dependence of metasurface often need to combine metasurface with traditional optical components [158], [193]. However, this integration method often has high requirements, such as the size of the metasurface being large enough, difficulty in manufacturing, and high production costs. Therefore, it is necessary to consider optimizing the properties of the metasurface itself to solve the existing problems. To improve the performance of metasurface under tshe premise of existing technology and reduce its design complexity, the future development direction of metasurface includes artificial intelligence (AI) assisted metasurface inverse design, adjoint algorithm-based optimization, flexible media tunable metasurface, cascade metasurface and quantum metasurface. In recent years, the inverse approach of AI-assisted design of metasurfaces, capable of designing arbitrary meta-atomic structures with higher DOFs, has been validated by advanced simulation optimization [194], [195] machine learning [196], and deep learning [197], [198]. AI-driven metasurface design has advanced rapidly through the integration of deep learning techniques such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and reinforcement learning (RL) [199]- [205]. GANs have been employed to generate highly complex, non-intuitive nanostructures for tasks like holography and beam shaping, achieving superior performance beyond traditional inverse design methods. For example, Jiang et al. demonstrated that GAN-generated diffractive metasurfaces could produce custom holographic projections with enhanced accuracy and efficiency [204]. In parallel, RL algorithms enable dynamic optimization of metasurface performance -such as polarization control or light efficiency -via iterative feedback, as shown by Sun et al., who optimized structural parameters while reducing fabrication complexity [205]. Together, these AI frameworks provide powerful, scalable solutions for tailoring metasurface functionalities in next-generation display and optical systems.
evidence_packets.source_title: Application of metasurface in future displays

exact_spans: The core challenge in metasurface engineering lies in the inverse design problem: determining the physical structure that produces a desired spectral response. This problem is mathematically ill-posed for two primary reasons. First, it is a one-to-many mapping; multiple distinct geometric configurations can yield identical optical spectra. This non-uniqueness confuses deterministic optimization algorithms and traditional regression-based neural networks, often leading to mode averaging and the generation of invalid geometries. Second, the mapping from geometry to spectrum is highly non-linear and governed by complex electromagnetic resonance modes [2]. While data-driven approaches using deep learning have emerged as a powerful alternative, they face significant hurdles. Generative models like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been employed to tackle the one-to-many mapping issue. However, these models operate primarily in the image or parameter domain and lack an intrinsic understanding of the underlying physics. Consequently, a generated structure might appear geometrically valid but fail to produce the target spectrum when verified with a Maxwell solver. This discrepancy, known as the simulation-reality gap, necessitates a design framework that is not only generative but also physics-informed, ensuring that the synthesized designs obey the fundamental laws of electromagnetics [3].
evidence_packets.source_title: Inverse Design of Metasurfaces Using Physics-Informed Diffusion Models with Spectral Constraints

exact_spans: The core objective of metasurface inverse design is as follows: given a target elec- tromagnetic response (e.g., a specific phase response in a frequency band), generate a metasurface structure that satisfies the requirement. However, this problem inherently exhibits a “one-to-many” characteristic—a single target response may correspond to in- finitely many physically feasible metasurface structures (e.g., different combinations of unit geometric parameters may achieve the same phase response). Traditional super- vised learning methods (e.g., CNN regression) typically learn only one “average solution,” which fails to cover the diversity of the solution space and results in design outcomes that are singular and lack innovativeness. The adversarial training mechanism of GANs (generator–discriminator game) addresses this issue by forcing the generator to learn the solution space distribution corresponding to the target response—to deceive the discrim- inator, the generator must not only produce a single “optimal solution” but also cover a broader range of “feasible solutions” (e.g., different unit sizes that still match the phase requirements). This mechanism enables GANs to output diverse metasurface structures, significantly enhancing the innovativeness of inverse design. Among them, the framework diagrams of metasurface design using GAN models in recent studies are shown in Figure 4. Figure 4a illustrates the architecture of the discriminator and generator in the DPN-GAN model [157]. Figure 4b demonstrates the overall workflow and framework of the Deep UCGAN+ model [386].
evidence_packets.source_title: Advances in Deep Learning-Driven Metasurface Design and Application in Holographic Imaging

exact_spans: This integrated approach mitigated the constraints of PSO related to DoFs and reduced the risk of converging on local minima, which is a common limitation in adjoint-based local optimization methods. 4.2. Gradient-based approaches Gradient-free optimization methods, including evolutionary optimization, often encounter significant computational demands when addressing complex design challenges because of their high-dimensional nature [ 64 ]. In scenarios where computational resources are a limiting factor, gradient-based optimization techniques can provide a more efficient solution for large-scale applications. Consequently, gradient-based strategies, such as the adjoint method [ 151 ], often in conjunction with topology optimization [ 22 ], have yielded numerous successful outcomes [ 126 ], [ 152 ] in inverse design tasks. The concept of topology optimization, particularly highlighted after Jensen and Sigmund’s groundbreaking introduction of its use in designing photonic crystal structures [ 153 ], [ 154 ], has since become a cornerstone in photonic device design, particularly for devices that require a high DoF. This method strategically segments the design space into computational elements or pixels, considering each as a distinct design parameter, thereby effectively increasing the DoFs of the system. In pursuit of superior device structures, the application of level-set and adjoint density-based topology optimization has been observed in studies conducted by Lalau-Keraly et al. [ 155 ], Borel et al. [ 156 ], Burger and Stanley [ 157 ], and Gerken and Miller [ 158 ].
evidence_packets.source_title: Large-scale photonic inverse design: computational challenges and breakthroughs

exact_spans: The traditional design process for multifunctional metasurfaces usually includes the following steps: 1. Senior experts propose a possible design plan that meets the design requirements, including the number of layers, medium type and thickness of the metasurface, and most importantly, the shape of the metal layer. 2. Abstract the design plan into a parameter space, and then enter a complex parameter scanning and itera- tion process to obtain a satisfactory solution. We can usually find a solution closest to the design requirements in this parameter space, but sometimes the gap between the optimal solution and the design goal still cannot satisfy us, requiring a redesign of the plan and then a parameter scanning and iteration. This is undoubtedly a time-consuming and frustrating process. The functional integration of metasurfaces makes this process even more complex and sometimes even impossible. Machine learning-based inverse design methods are emerg- ing as effective alternatives to artificial metasurface design.[15,16] These methods leverage powerful fitting capabilities and rapid searching abilities in ultra-large solution spaces. Significant progress has been made in the field of electromagnetic metasur- face inverse design based on artificial intelligence. Early stud- ies primarily focused on classic metasurface structures, such as cross-shaped,[17–19] cylindrical,[20] H-shaped,[20,21] and other fixed shapes.[22,23] These structures have fixed geometric shapes Adv. exact_spans: Designing metasurfaces for tailored optical functions is an inherently inverse problem in a high-dimensional, nonconvex space. Traditional methods such as particle swarm optimization [23] and genetic algorithms [24] are computationally intensive and non-differentiable, which hinders end-to-end integration with downstream tasks. Recent datadriven approaches leverage deep neural networks as efficient surrogates for electromagnetic solvers [18], [19], [20], though they often face challenges ensuring physical realizability. Our work builds on these advances by introducing a neural simulator trained on over 320,000 GSST metasurface geometries with spectral responses across 11 crystallization states. Using a Transformer-based architecture [25], [26], the simulator accurately maps geometric features to spectral behavior and, being fully differentiable, enables gradientbased optimization of both the metasurface and the spectral reconstruction network [27]. Additionally, our novel soft shape regularization technique ensures that the optimized designs remain physically realizable [28], addressing one of the key challenges in bridging computational design with practical fabrication constraints.

current_section_boundary_contract.title: Active Modulation Mechanisms for Dynamic Metasurface Holography: Speed, Efficiency, and Spectral Trade-offs
current_section_boundary_contract.handoff_from_previous: Having established the static fabrication baseline, the review now introduces active modulation as the pathway to dynamic holographic operation, examining how each mechanism modifies the phase profile in real time for metasurface holography.
current_section_boundary_contract.handoff_to_next: With active modulation mechanisms characterized, the review examines how these dynamic holographic metasurfaces are integrated into display architectures and evaluated against application-specific performance criteria for metasurface holography.

sibling_section_responsibilities.title: Phase Control Mechanisms in Metasurface Holography: Foundations and Limits
sibling_section_responsibilities.summary: Establishes the three fundamental phase control mechanisms—geometric phase, propagation phase, and hybrid approaches—that underpin all metasurface holographic wavefront engineering, and characterizes their intrinsic trade-offs in efficiency, bandwidth, polarization sensitivity, and design flexibility that constrain every downstream application domain.

sibling_section_responsibilities.title: Computational Inverse Design for Metasurface Holograms: From Forward Models to Algorithmic Optimization
sibling_section_responsibilities.summary: Demonstrates that computational inverse design has evolved from simple superposition-based hologram encoding to sophisticated algorithmic optimization including gradient-based, topology optimization, and machine learning methods, but that these methods operate on idealized nanostructure models that ignore fabrication-induced disorder and modulation constraints, creating a design-reality gap that propagates through the entire metasurface holography pipeline.

sibling_section_responsibilities.title: Nanofabrication of Metasurface Holograms: Tolerances, Disorder, and Scalability
sibling_section_responsibilities.summary: Establishes that nanofabrication processes impose tolerance thresholds and introduce structural disorder that systematically degrade holographic fidelity below design predictions for metasurface holograms, and that scalable manufacturing strategies capable of producing meter-scale holographic metasurfaces remain largely unvalidated compared to lab-scale e-beam lithography demonstrations.

sibling_section_responsibilities.title: Metasurface Holographic Displays: Architectures, Metrics, and Application Readiness
sibling_section_responsibilities.summary: Evaluates how metasurface-based holographic displays integrate static or dynamically modulated metasurfaces into complete display systems, assesses performance against established holographic display metrics including viewing angle, color gamut, refresh rate, brightness, and eye-box size, and identifies which application niches are closest to commercial readiness versus which remain constrained by unresolved mechanism trade-offs in metasurface holography.

sibling_section_responsibilities.title: Metasurface-Integrated Imaging Systems and Optical Computing: Beyond Display Applications
sibling_section_responsibilities.summary: Examines how metasurface holography extends beyond display applications into computational imaging, metalens-based holographic microscopy, beam steering for LiDAR and free-space communications, and optical computing architectures, demonstrating that these applications impose different performance priorities such as resolution, field of view, and channel count that reveal additional facets of the mechanism-coupling problem in metasurface holography.

sibling_section_responsibilities.title: Cross-Cutting Challenges and Co-Design Strategies in Metasurface Holography: Resolving the Coupled Mechanism Bottleneck
sibling_section_responsibilities.summary: Synthesizes the review's central argument by identifying where the metasurface holography literature shows genuine disagreement rather than mere incompleteness of evidence, where controversies persist regarding which phase control mechanisms should dominate future designs and whether top-down or bottom-up fabrication will win for scalable holography, and what co-design strategies involving joint optimization of design, fabrication tolerance, and modulation constraints are emerging to resolve the coupled mechanism bottleneck in metasurface holography.

research_context.user_question: This research inquiry seeks to systematically map the complete technological pipeline of metasurface-based holography, addressing how computational inverse design algorithms optimize nanostructure geometry for wavefront control, how scalable nanofabrication processes translate these designs into physical devices, and how active modulation mechanisms enable real-time dynamic holographic displays and advanced imaging systems.
research_context.scope_definition: ['Focus on active modulation mechanisms specifically applied to holographic metasurfaces; exclude tunable metasurfaces for non-holographic applications', 'Cover all major active platforms: phase-change materials (GST, VO2), liquid crystals, MEMS, graphene, electro-optic polymers, thermo-optic materials', 'Do not re-cover static phase control from S01 or fabrication from S03', 'Do not discuss system-level display integration here—reserve for S05']
research_context.global_review_thesis: Metasurface holography has demonstrated remarkable capability in static wavefront engineering, yet its transition to real-time dynamic displays and advanced imaging systems remains incomplete. This review argues that the field's central bottleneck is not any single technological component but the uncoupled treatment of design, fabrication, and modulation: inverse design algorithms optimize idealized nanostructures without accounting for fabrication tolerances, nanofabrication processes introduce disorder that degrades holographic fidelity, and active modulation mechanisms sacrifice diffraction efficiency or spectral bandwidth for speed. By organizing the literature around these three coupled mechanisms, this review identifies where independent optimization succeeds, where cross-mechanism trade-offs dominate, and what co-design strategies are emerging to bridge these gaps. The synthesis reveals that while individual components have reached impressive benchmarks, system-level performance in dynamic holographic displays and integrated imaging remains limited by unresolved tensions among efficiency, bandwidth, resolution, and refresh rate—tensions that demand joint design-fabrication-modulation approaches rather than sequential optimization.
research_context.global_narrative_strategy: Demonstrates that active modulation mechanisms spanning phase-change materials, liquid crystals, MEMS actuators, graphene, and electro-optic polymers enable real-time holographic reconfiguration but each imposes distinct penalties on diffraction efficiency, spectral bandwidth, or modulation depth, creating a fundamental speed-efficiency-bandwidth trilemma that constrains practical dynamic metasurface holographic displays.

# Metasurface Holographic Displays: Architectures, Metrics, and Application Readiness

Inverse design serves as the foundational computational strategy for navigating the high-dimensional parameter spaces inherent to nanophotonic metasurfaces, effectively replacing intuition-based heuristics with mathematical optimization to achieve complex wavefront modulation. [REF:doi:10.48550/arxiv.2505.18377] Unlike classical iterative methods that often suffer from excessive computational consumption when addressing multi-objective or multi-scale challenges, deep learning-based approaches model intricate physical relationships between material properties and optical responses, enabling the rapid convergence of design parameters. This paradigm shift is exemplified by frameworks such as MOCLIP, a foundation model that leverages a shared latent space to embed metasurface geometries and spectra jointly, achieving inference speeds approximately thirty times faster than traditional computational electrodynamic strategies while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, hybrid architectures integrate neural networks with adjoint-based gradient evaluation, utilizing affine geometric transformations to optimize multiple meta-atom parameters simultaneously, thereby reducing complexity without sacrificing the ability to explore diverse design configurations. While these advanced algorithms successfully generate the static profiles required for high-quality holographic control, they establish only the geometric prerequisite for display systems; the subsequent challenge lies in overcoming the non-uniqueness and generalization failures that arise when these static designs must be adapted for dynamic, physics-constrained environments. [REF:2d3412a215f8b6d1d395bfaeec7ec0379c2e132e] [REF:2326997ee1d85fcb31f51c4488cdfaa40639d131] [REF:a801ee6d75d827ef0b99528619e877e3aac72277] [REF:e4817fc664074ddc772d9ae198871fc6cb7f8b7b]

While inverse design provides the necessary framework for navigating high-dimensional parameter spaces, standard data-driven neural networks often fail when confronted with the ill-posed nature of metasurface engineering, where multiple distinct geometric configurations can yield identical optical spectra. This non-uniqueness confuses deterministic algorithms and leads to invalid geometries that lack physical realizability. To resolve this, physics-informed machine learning integrates governing physical equations, such as Maxwell's electromagnetic wave equations, directly into neural network loss functions or architectures. [REF:doi:10.48550/arxiv.2312.06177] [REF:doi:10.48550/arxiv.2606.04143] By penalizing predictions that violate conservation laws or symmetry requirements, these models act as regularizers that reduce the search space and ensure generated structures obey fundamental electromagnetics, thereby closing the simulation-reality gap inherent in purely generative approaches. Furthermore, hybrid algorithms have emerged to overcome the generalization limits of neural networks beyond their training datasets by combining deep learning with conventional optimization methods like the adjoint variables method. In this synergistic pipeline, the neural network performs a rapid global search to provide an ideal initial condition, which iterative optimization algorithms then refine through local searches to achieve optimal performance. [REF:doi:10.3390/math13040631] [REF:doi:10.54392/irjmt2511] These advanced frameworks transform inverse design from a black-box prediction tool into a robust methodology capable of generating explainable, high-fidelity metasurfaces, setting the stage for specific architectural innovations that further accelerate the design-to-fabrication pipeline. [REF:0d03f30ab91ec0b9411c3e2505550e636df8808e] [REF:0c04bf631766f465f0b30dcd07a342ff014ed8f3] [REF:9c20a790aa75f24b6f5a130711645c978484455e]

Building on the physics-aware foundations established previously, specific network topologies now directly tackle the non-uniqueness and data inefficiency that plague standard inverse design. Deep neural networks employing tandem architectures address the one-to-many mapping problem inherent in inverse scattering, where multiple geometries can produce identical optical responses; by structuring the network to learn this complex relationship, researchers facilitate the faster realization of functional metasurfaces through transfer learning paradigms that leverage large training sets of up to 500,000 instances. [REF:doi:10.1209/0295-5075/ad3a0f] [REF:doi:10.1364/oe.398926] Complementing this, generative models and deep learning-based approaches significantly reduce the data requirements and iteration counts needed to optimize nanophotonic elements, accelerating the development cycle for complex holographic displays by minimizing validation processes. Furthermore, because practical inverse-design problems are frequently under-constrained or subject to dynamic objectives like shifting fabrication limits, representation learning techniques have emerged to mitigate these challenges. These methods create reusable, physics-agnostic manifolds of device geometries and fast surrogate solvers, enabling efficient exploration and rapid re-optimization when constraints evolve. To further enhance sample efficiency in freeform device optimization, physics-informed reinforcement learning combines physical information from adjoint-based methods with deep RL agents, allowing for the discovery of optimal devices in vast combinatorial design spaces with reduced variance. Collectively, these architectural innovations shift the bottleneck from geometric complexity to computational tractability, setting the stage for integrating these optimized static designs into compact physical system architectures. [REF:a881bff2781bda627de54299c45a6708d145c27a] [REF:fa86aab8916cbb533d714bce5861b01dabbf18cb] [REF:1710ffd8f90365fdbef063f85605601e2c7fc9f1] [REF:77dd2a80bc5f7d1504a411a519cae5c5e5074099]

Building on the accelerated design-to-fabrication pipelines enabled by advanced network topologies, the physical realization of metasurface holographic displays has evolved from isolated components into diverse system architectures. These displays are primarily implemented in transmissive and reflective configurations, which leverage sub-wavelength control over light waves to achieve ultra-miniaturization essential for consumer displays and near-eye applications. Recent demonstrations have expanded this landscape to include projection systems and integrated adaptive devices; for instance, researchers have realized broadband dynamic camouflage cloaks by integrating microfluidics to modulate liquid metal within meta-atoms, representing a significant step toward multi-illusion components. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of standalone diffractive elements, hybrid meta-refractive lens architectures have emerged as a viable pathway for compact integration. In these systems, traditional refractive elements provide the bulk optical power while metasurfaces correct specific aberrations, a strategy that has improved average focusing efficiency from 38% to over 90% in midwave infrared lenses by flexibly interleaving optical elements. This capacity for miniaturization is further evidenced in endoscopic imaging, where hybrid meta-GRIN lens systems have achieved substantial contrast improvements without the complex assembly of multiple refractive lenses. However, despite these architectural advances, the chapter thesis remains constrained by the difficulty of scaling these static or slowly reconfigurable designs into high-frame-rate commercial systems, as current manufacturing complexities and material losses still hinder the infinite frame rates required for seamless optical information display. [REF:dfa21cd70a71ab37879ca600843b21680f16e478] [REF:2a1ac67eb9a6793168e50de6831ae02c5372b6b6] [REF:83b6d6523c4d30208870b774f116709b04fd7b4b] [REF:d54b94b2ee8549d7ab4bf6ec47e0259df06a047a]

While compact system architectures address form factor, achieving full-color operation requires overcoming the fundamental challenge of chromatic dispersion. Multilayer optical thin film structures provide a foundational photonic platform for broadband metasurface operation, where stacking layers with thicknesses ranging from tens to hundreds of nanometers enables precise control over light interference and spectral responses. In augmented reality displays, a common strategy to eliminate chromatic dispersion without compromising the field of view involves utilizing three separate waveguides, each dedicated to red, green, and blue channels. However, this tri-waveguide approach inherently increases system complexity and cost while introducing risks of ghost images and reduced modulation transfer function due to misalignment. To mitigate these issues, recent advances propose achromatic metasurface waveguides that utilize ultra-thin silicon nitride nanostructure couplers integrated into a single-plate waveguide. This design leverages different diffraction orders for RGB wavelengths in reflection mode to achieve high color and angular uniformity, offering a viable, cost-effective solution to longstanding aberration issues. Although limitations such as wavelength mismatches and polarization selectivity remain, this integration of advanced inverse design with specific waveguide architectures exemplifies the balance between static precision and system-level constraints necessary for commercial viability. [REF:42e53c9c7630eb735f9a67f329c948423910cd8d] [REF:94ab4c73d8ea40f73635551d123a18a300d824cb]

While inverse design has successfully navigated the geometric complexity required for sophisticated wavefront shaping, the resulting devices often remain constrained by their physical nature as static metasurfaces. These conventional devices possess an intrinsic "write-once" characteristic where optical functions are fixed upon fabrication, severely restricting their adaptability and flexibility in dynamic scenarios compared to reconfigurable alternatives. Although researchers have attempted to endow metasurfaces with dynamic tunability using active materials or mechanical displacement, these approaches often introduce significant hurdles such as high optical loss, fabrication complexity, or reliance on bulky mechanical actuators. This limitation persists even in advanced resonant architectures that exploit bound states in the continuum (BICs) to support high-quality factor resonances and electric field confinement by restraining radiation losses. For instance, nonlocal Huygens' meta-lenses can achieve high quality factors and efficient polarization conversion for multiplexing imaging, yet these capabilities are typically demonstrated in static or slowly modulated contexts rather than high-refresh-rate video. Similarly, while humidity-modulated strategies can regulate the dynamic transition from quasi-BICs to BICs through symmetry breaking, such mechanisms rely on specific environmental stimuli and reaction kinetics that differ fundamentally from the rapid electronic switching required for real-time holographic displays. Consequently, the translation of complex static designs into dynamic systems remains bottlenecked not by the geometric design process itself, but by the speed and efficiency of the underlying active modulation mechanisms, reinforcing the chapter's thesis that commercial viability requires integrating advanced design algorithms with architectures that specifically balance static precision against dynamic constraints. [REF:d3a8c619f7797527ae0f94573705a517d9aad779] [REF:2a537b9b3aec2380ca8343d8bd5cc70e6d974970] [REF:cc73f5040c5d928b3ca5aeeb38e0df04450efc53]

Building on the recognition that dynamic modulation remains a primary bottleneck, the immediate commercial trajectory of metasurface holography favors high-complexity static architectures where inverse design can fully resolve inter-channel crosstalk and efficiency losses. As design complexity increases, challenges related to crosstalk between different channels and overall work efficiency necessitate continuous improvement, often driving the integration of metasurfaces with traditional optical components despite manufacturing difficulties and high production costs. To overcome these limitations without relying solely on bulky hybrid systems, deep-learning-assisted inverse design has emerged as a critical enabler for creating dual-spin and dual-frequency metasurfaces capable of quad-channel off-axis holographic multiplexing. This approach utilizes specialized neural networks, including classifiers and artificial neural networks (ANNs), to automatically output the specific physical parameters required to suppress cross-talk in both geometric and propagation phases, thereby allowing independent control over multiple spatial channels within a single static device. Furthermore, inverse design methodologies such as adjoint optimization extend beyond standalone flat optics to correct aberrations in hybrid systems, numerically demonstrating improved image quality when combining designed metasurfaces with bulk midwave infrared lenses. While these advances validate the use of AI-driven frameworks like generative adversarial networks and reinforcement learning for tailoring functionalities in next-generation displays, the reliance on static or slowly tunable configurations confirms that near-term market readiness lies primarily in augmented reality waveguides and security features rather than high-speed video displays. [REF:dfa21cd70a71ab37879ca600843b21680f16e478] [REF:867c87ae195e0a5c2016732e0f43a8c703a7a788] [REF:eb05cd6cdf1599f09588017b728231838003c121]

paragraphs.text: # Metasurface Holographic Displays: Architectures, Metrics, and Application Readiness

Inverse design serves as the foundational computational strategy for navigating the high-dimensional parameter spaces inherent to nanophotonic metasurfaces, effectively replacing intuition-based heuristics with mathematical optimization to achieve complex wavefront modulation. [REF:doi:10.48550/arxiv.2505.18377] Unlike classical iterative methods that often suffer from excessive computational consumption when addressing multi-objective or multi-scale challenges, deep learning-based approaches model intricate physical relationships between material properties and optical responses, enabling the rapid convergence of design parameters. This paradigm shift is exemplified by frameworks such as MOCLIP, a foundation model that leverages a shared latent space to embed metasurface geometries and spectra jointly, achieving inference speeds approximately thirty times faster than traditional computational electrodynamic strategies while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, hybrid architectures integrate neural networks with adjoint-based gradient evaluation, utilizing affine geometric transformations to optimize multiple meta-atom parameters simultaneously, thereby reducing complexity without sacrificing the ability to explore diverse design configurations. While these advanced algorithms successfully generate the static profiles required for high-quality holographic control, they establish only the geometric prerequisite for display systems; the subsequent challenge lies in overcoming the non-uniqueness and generalization failures that arise when these static designs must be adapted for dynamic, physics-constrained environments. [REF:2d3412a215f8b6d1d395bfaeec7ec0379c2e132e] [REF:2326997ee1d85fcb31f51c4488cdfaa40639d131] [REF:a801ee6d75d827ef0b99528619e877e3aac72277] [REF:e4817fc664074ddc772d9ae198871fc6cb7f8b7b]

While inverse design provides the necessary framework for navigating high-dimensional parameter spaces, standard data-driven neural networks often fail when confronted with the ill-posed nature of metasurface engineering, where multiple distinct geometric configurations can yield identical optical spectra. This non-uniqueness confuses deterministic algorithms and leads to invalid geometries that lack physical realizability. To resolve this, physics-informed machine learning integrates governing physical equations, such as Maxwell's electromagnetic wave equations, directly into neural network loss functions or architectures. [REF:doi:10.48550/arxiv.2312.06177] [REF:doi:10.48550/arxiv.2606.04143] By penalizing predictions that violate conservation laws or symmetry requirements, these models act as regularizers that reduce the search space and ensure generated structures obey fundamental electromagnetics, thereby closing the simulation-reality gap inherent in purely generative approaches. Furthermore, hybrid algorithms have emerged to overcome the generalization limits of neural networks beyond their training datasets by combining deep learning with conventional optimization methods like the adjoint variables method. In this synergistic pipeline, the neural network performs a rapid global search to provide an ideal initial condition, which iterative optimization algorithms then refine through local searches to achieve optimal performance. [REF:doi:10.3390/math13040631] [REF:doi:10.54392/irjmt2511] These advanced frameworks transform inverse design from a black-box prediction tool into a robust methodology capable of generating explainable, high-fidelity metasurfaces, setting the stage for specific architectural innovations that further accelerate the design-to-fabrication pipeline. [REF:0d03f30ab91ec0b9411c3e2505550e636df8808e] [REF:0c04bf631766f465f0b30dcd07a342ff014ed8f3] [REF:9c20a790aa75f24b6f5a130711645c978484455e]

Building on the physics-aware foundations established previously, specific network topologies now directly tackle the non-uniqueness and data inefficiency that plague standard inverse design. Deep neural networks employing tandem architectures address the one-to-many mapping problem inherent in inverse scattering, where multiple geometries can produce identical optical responses; by structuring the network to learn this complex relationship, researchers facilitate the faster realization of functional metasurfaces through transfer learning paradigms that leverage large training sets of up to 500,000 instances. [REF:doi:10.1209/0295-5075/ad3a0f] [REF:doi:10.1364/oe.398926] Complementing this, generative models and deep learning-based approaches significantly reduce the data requirements and iteration counts needed to optimize nanophotonic elements, accelerating the development cycle for complex holographic displays by minimizing validation processes. Furthermore, because practical inverse-design problems are frequently under-constrained or subject to dynamic objectives like shifting fabrication limits, representation learning techniques have emerged to mitigate these challenges. These methods create reusable, physics-agnostic manifolds of device geometries and fast surrogate solvers, enabling efficient exploration and rapid re-optimization when constraints evolve. To further enhance sample efficiency in freeform device optimization, physics-informed reinforcement learning combines physical information from adjoint-based methods with deep RL agents, allowing for the discovery of optimal devices in vast combinatorial design spaces with reduced variance. Collectively, these architectural innovations shift the bottleneck from geometric complexity to computational tractability, setting the stage for integrating these optimized static designs into compact physical system architectures. [REF:a881bff2781bda627de54299c45a6708d145c27a] [REF:fa86aab8916cbb533d714bce5861b01dabbf18cb] [REF:1710ffd8f90365fdbef063f85605601e2c7fc9f1] [REF:77dd2a80bc5f7d1504a411a519cae5c5e5074099]

Building on the accelerated design-to-fabrication pipelines enabled by advanced network topologies, the physical realization of metasurface holographic displays has evolved from isolated components into diverse system architectures. These displays are primarily implemented in transmissive and reflective configurations, which leverage sub-wavelength control over light waves to achieve ultra-miniaturization essential for consumer displays and near-eye applications. Recent demonstrations have expanded this landscape to include projection systems and integrated adaptive devices; for instance, researchers have realized broadband dynamic camouflage cloaks by integrating microfluidics to modulate liquid metal within meta-atoms, representing a significant step toward multi-illusion components. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of standalone diffractive elements, hybrid meta-refractive lens architectures have emerged as a viable pathway for compact integration. In these systems, traditional refractive elements provide the bulk optical power while metasurfaces correct specific aberrations, a strategy that has improved average focusing efficiency from 38% to over 90% in midwave infrared lenses by flexibly interleaving optical elements. This capacity for miniaturization is further evidenced in endoscopic imaging, where hybrid meta-GRIN lens systems have achieved substantial contrast improvements without the complex assembly of multiple refractive lenses. However, despite these architectural advances, the chapter thesis remains constrained by the difficulty of scaling these static or slowly reconfigurable designs into high-frame-rate commercial systems, as current manufacturing complexities and material losses still hinder the infinite frame rates required for seamless optical information display. [REF:dfa21cd70a71ab37879ca600843b21680f16e478] [REF:2a1ac67eb9a6793168e50de6831ae02c5372b6b6] [REF:83b6d6523c4d30208870b774f116709b04fd7b4b] [REF:d54b94b2ee8549d7ab4bf6ec47e0259df06a047a]

key_questions: What display architectures have been demonstrated using metasurface holograms including transmissive, reflective, projection, and AR/VR-integrated configurations?
How do current metasurface holographic displays perform against standard holographic display metrics compared to competing technologies such as SLM-based, volumetric, and integral imaging approaches?
What system-level integration challenges arise when combining metasurface holograms with light sources, drivers, and control electronics?

Which application domains including consumer displays, AR/VR headsets, automotive HUDs, and medical visualization show the clearest path to adoption and what remaining barriers exist for metasurface holography?
section_contract.synthesis_task: Synthesize a readiness assessment of metasurface holographic displays across application domains, distinguishing demonstrations that meet application requirements from those that remain at proof-of-concept stage, and identifying which mechanism trade-offs are the primary barriers to each application domain in metasurface holography.
section_contract.title: Metasurface Holographic Displays: Architectures, Metrics, and Application Readiness
section_contract.central_thesis: Evaluate how metasurface-based holographic displays integrate static or dynamically modulated metasurfaces into complete display systems, assess performance against established holographic display metrics (viewing angle, color gamut, refresh rate, brightness, eye-box size), and identify which application niches are closest to commercial readiness versus which remain constrained by unresolved mechanism trade-offs.
section_contract.section_purpose: Evaluates how metasurface-based holographic displays integrate static or dynamically modulated metasurfaces into complete display systems, assesses performance against established holographic display metrics including viewing angle, color gamut, refresh rate, brightness, and eye-box size, and identifies which application niches are closest to commercial readiness versus which remain constrained by unresolved mechanism trade-offs in metasurface holography.

Include both static and dynamic display demonstrations
